title: Sparse Carleman Embeddings for Nonlinear Discrete Dynamical Systems
abstract: Discrete nonlinear dynamical systems arise in population models, iterative optimization, and numerical simulations, where computing many iterations can be costly in high dimensions. We study Carleman embedding for forced quadratic discrete systems and its application to quantum state preparation. Under explicit stability and initial-state assumptions, we prove that the truncation error decreases geometrically with the embedding degree, uniformly over all iterations. A central obstacle in discrete time is that the lifted update can become dense even when the original coefficient maps are sparse. We overcome this obstacle by constructing an exact auxiliary linear-system representation that applies the coefficient maps one tensor factor at a time, with row and column sparsities bounded independently of the truncation degree. After rescaling, the associated history system has a condition number that grows linearly with the iteration count, uniformly in the truncation degree. These results yield a quantum algorithm for preparing an approximation to the normalized $n$th iterate with constant success probability. Under coherent input-access assumptions, and for fixed sparsity, stability parameters, and a known positive lower bound on the final-state norm, the oracle query complexity is linear in $n$ and polylogarithmic in the inverse accuracy. Numerical experiments in one and three dimensions illustrate the convergence of the truncated embedding.

title: Decoding with alternating weighted graph sparsification for quantum low-density parity-check codes
abstract: Real-time decoding is a fundamental necessity for building fault-tolerant quantum computers. In this work, we introduce decoding with alternating weighted graph sparsification (DAWG), an ensemble based approach that combines Tanner graph sparsification with ensembling belief-propagation (BP) decoders. The DAWG decoder runs BP decoders over the full detector error model Tanner graph for certain iterations to then transfer the posteriors to a sparsified graph in which additional rounds of BP are run. Each of the decoders in the ensemble uses a different transfer matrix to map the posterior information to the sparsified graph. We use the serial schedule for the minimum-sum BP decoders and, thus, employ Vibe decoding ideas by randomizing the schedules of each of them. The performance of the DAWG decoder is then numerically studied for bivariate bicycle codes and superdense color code circuits to be compared with other state-of-the-art decoding approaches. Importantly, the DAWG decoder shows a similar performance to Relay belief-propagation and Vibe decoding when combined with an order-$0$ Localized Statistics Decoding (LSD-$0$) post-processor. Crucially, the post-processor is called an order of magnitude less times than for Vibe with the same ensemble size, indicating that the introduced latency tail will be minimal. Furthermore, LSD-$0$ operates on a sparsified decoding graph of a fraction of the size of the full detector error model, which simplifies the resources required by specialized hardware to support it. Overall, the DAWG+LSD-$0$ decoder represents a viable low-cost BP-based decoding algorithm for quantum error correction codes.

title: Parametrically Enhanced Ergotropy and Charging Power in a Three-Mode Bosonic Quantum Battery
abstract: Quantum batteries are quantum systems that potentially serve as fuel for other quantum devices by receiving and supplying energy. In this work, we propose a theoretical scheme to enhance ergotropy and charging power of quantum Battery in the system under consideration through squeezed light. Moreover, The system comprises a coherently driven charger cavity, a strongly dissipative auxiliary cavity acting as a mediator, and an energy--storage battery cavity. Quantum nonreciprocity and directional energy flow are established via destructive quantum interference between the direct coupling path and the loss--engineered indirect path. A degenerate optical parametric amplifier integrated into the charger cavity acts as an active, phase--sensitive energy source that injects two--photon quantum excitations and anomalous correlations. Using a strictly open--quantum--system framework derived directly from the Lindblad master equation, we obtain the full expectation--value dynamics and stationary states. We show that active parametric driving drastically increases the stored energy and peak charging power while maintaining nonreciprocal energy trapping in the battery. We achieve a multi-order-of-magnitude boost in the battery's stored energy, charging power, and ergotropy. We also analyze the effects of pure dephasing on the charging power, ergotropy, and extractable work quality.. Although two--photon pumping introduces photon--number fluctuations that slightly lower the fractional ergotropy ratio ${\cal W}_{\rm B}/{\cal E}_{\rm B}$, the absolute extractable work remains substantially elevated compared to unassisted configurations.

title: Quantum computation of energy level degeneracy and thermodynamical properties of spin systems
abstract:
We propose a hybrid quantum-classical method for reconstructing energy-level degeneracies and thermodynamic properties of spin systems. A single ancilla qubit is used to measure the partition function at imaginary inverse temperatures. For spectra lying on a known equally spaced energy grid, the inverse discrete Fourier transform allows exact reconstruction of degeneracies in the absence of noise, without spectral leakage. The quantum circuits are optimized using commuting interactions and Eulerian ordering. We demonstrate the method for frustrated Ising antiferromagnets on periodic Kagome graphs with up to 36 spins, using the ibm_kingston quantum processor. Despite substantial circuit depth and hardware noise, the reconstructed spectra retain their dominant features, and the calculated heat capacities reproduce the main temperature dependence of the exact results.

title: Fast and accurate rare-event simulation by Markov chain Monte Carlo for general quantum codes
abstract: The splitting method estimates logical error rates of quantum error-correcting codes deep in the rare-event regime, where direct Monte Carlo sampling is prohibitively expensive. It relies on a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampler of faulty configurations, usually driven by one-bit-flip proposals. However, one-bit flips have been reported to be trapped on some codes, which biases the estimate. To address this issue, we propose a new kernel that combines locally balanced one-bit-flip proposals with a cluster-exchange move. We benchmark both kernels and direct Monte Carlo on twelve codes under code-capacity bit-flip noise in two ways, by comparing the mean fault weight with an MCMC-independent reference and by measuring the computation time to reach a fixed accuracy. In the first, our kernel agrees with the reference on every code, including those where one-bit flips are trapped. In the second, it is faster than one-bit flips wherever they are trapped, by orders of magnitude on some codes. Furthermore, at the lowest error rate, it is faster than direct Monte Carlo on every code, by more than four orders of magnitude on some.

title: Multipartite dynamics beyond bipartite entanglement equilibration
abstract: Entanglement equilibration need not mark the end of quantum-information dynamics in quantum thermalization. We show that the complete Schmidt spectra of a fixed tripartition can become stationary while its multipartite correlation structure, distinguished by local-unitary invariants, continues to evolve. This separation occurs exactly within a finite window in self-dual kicked-Ising dynamics and asymptotically in Haar-random circuits. We further demonstrate an independently tunable timescale for multipartite dynamics using quantum-error-correcting codes. When coupled to a locally scrambling bath, ordinary entanglement approaches equilibrium through rapid local scrambling, while weak logical--bath coupling drives a slower reorganization of multipartite correlations. These results reveal a deeper distinction than the ordering of equilibration times: bipartite entanglement and multipartite correlation structure can probe distinct physical channels of quantum-information dynamics, rather than merely different stages of the same relaxation process.

title: Spectral fingerprint recognition of mobile signals via Rydberg atomic sensors
abstract: Rydberg-atom sensors have emerged as a promising quantum technology for broadband radio-frequency detection owing to their intrinsic calibration, wide frequency coverage, and high sensitivity. However, their potential for intelligent identification of real-world wireless signals remains largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate a quantum-enabled framework for mobile signal classification based on Rydberg electromagnetically induced transparency spectroscopy and deep learning. Three types of wireless emissions, including cellular voice call, Wi-Fi, and 5G signals from three commercial smartphone brands, are measured to construct a spectral-fingerprint dataset. A convolutional neural network trained on this dataset achieves an initial baseline classification accuracy of 93.44\%. To compensate for spectral drifts induced by temporal and environmental variations, a progressive fine-tuning strategy is employed to continuously adapt the pretrained model, enabling robust classification across diverse deployment scenarios. Furthermore, continuous real-time monitoring is demonstrated under dynamically varying wireless conditions, including cellular voice call, Wi-Fi, and their coexistence. The proposed system achieves an overall frame-level recognition accuracy of 87.67\% over a 60-s measurement. These results establish a pathway toward intelligent quantum radio-frequency sensing and highlight the potential of Rydberg-atom platforms for real-time wireless signal awareness and spectrum monitoring.

title: Bargmann-invariant witness of the graviton commutator
abstract: We identify the phase of a Bargmann invariant of two matter-wave interferometers as a quantum gravity signature that cannot be reproduced by any branchwise-definite classical gravitational field. For matter coupled linearly to linearized gravity, the interferometric coherence factorizes exactly into a conservative Newtonian phase, the characteristic functional of the graviton state, and a commutator phase. For Wigner-positive graviton states, the first two are classically reproducible; therefore, decoherence alone cannot certify that gravity is quantized. The Bargmann phase isolates the commutator, which is independent of the graviton state and of all Newtonian interactions and is bounded by which-path decoherence. For gravity, this radiation-reaction effect is sixty orders of magnitude below experimental reach, but trapped-ion analogs can test it at order unity.

title: A Control Line Multiplexing Framework for Scalable Quantum Computing
abstract: Universal fault-tolerant superconducting quantum computers are expected to require millions of physical qubits; yet extending the prevailing dedicated-control-line paradigm to this scale would exceed the wiring density and cooling-power budget of dilution refrigerators. Microwave frequency-division multiplexing (FDM) revolutionized classical communications by enabling many independent channels to share common transmission infrastructure. Translating this principle to superconducting quantum control, however, requires an all-microwave architecture and experimental validation of frequency-multiplexed gate control. Recent work in quantum error correction has demonstrated microwave-based readout, single-qubit gates and leakage suppression, whereas two-qubit gates remain predominantly driven by unipolar pulses and thus constitute the missing element of an all-microwave architecture. Here, we propose a periodically extensible hybrid multiplexing framework in which all gate operations are frequency-division multiplexed using polychromatic microwave pulses and band-pass filters, thereby reducing the required control-line count by one to two orders of magnitude. In a 1:4 demonstration, we achieve average errors of $(6.4\pm0.2)\times10^{-3}$ for parallel FDM CZ gates and $(10.6\pm0.2)\times10^{-4}$ for parallel FDM $XY(π/2)$ gates, without statistically significant multiplexing-induced degradation. Together with on-chip DC sources, this FDM-based gate-control scheme completes the last missing module in a scalable multiplexed-control architecture toward universal fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Basis-set error bounds for first-quantised quantum simulation of chemistry
abstract: In quantum simulation of electronic structure it is often expected that the estimate of the ground energy converges to the continuum basis limit at a rate of $\mathcal O(N^{-1})$ for a basis of size $N$. This has been found in analytical and numerical studies, but without a rigorous treatment of the error in the quantities considered in quantum algorithms. Here we show the $\mathcal O(N^{-1})$ scaling of the error for a wide range of cases needed for quantum simulation of chemistry. We show the error in the ground energy scales as $\mathcal O(N^{-1})$ for plane-wave as well as spatial grid bases. For the spatial grid we consider both a periodic system and a non-periodic system with open boundaries. For time evolution, our bound on the error in the state itself is weaker than $\mathcal O(N^{-1})$, but we show that the error in observables scales as $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(N^{-1})$ in important cases. In particular, we may consider a smoothed observable that describes the position of particles. We show that this error scales as $\mathcal O(N^{-5/3}+tN^{-1})$ for time $t$, again both for plane-wave and spatial grid bases. For the non-periodic grid case we use a condition that the true evolution would not result in significant leakage past the boundaries, which introduces basis error unrelated to the resolution of the discretisation. We also show the error in the kinetic energy of a particle scales as $\mathcal O((t+\log N)/N)$ for the plane-wave and grid bases. Together, these results show that $\mathcal O(N^{-1})$ scaling of the error holds for many of the relevant cases for quantum algorithms (with a trivial log factor for kinetic energy).

title: Neutrinos as Quantum Information Carriers? A Gap Analysis Against the DiVincenzo Criteria
abstract: Photons, trapped ions, neutral atoms, and superconducting circuits are all well-known quantum information platforms. Neutrinos offer a unique possibility, displaying quantum interference (flavour oscillation) over thousands of kilometres, yet interacting so weakly that they can travel through the Earth with minimal interaction. This short paper is a gap analysis. We use information from the existing literature to compare neutrinos to the seven DiVincenzo requirements. Firstly, there are five requirements to do with computation and secondly two requirements to do with communication. We analyse where the gaps are for each requirement. Overall, we find that neutrinos have high fidelity and good coherence; however, they do not have a clear qubit definition and initialisation. They do not have universal gates, individual qubit readout, or stationary-to-flying conversion, meaning they either fail or are very poor. Therefore, we think they are best considered as an exceptional flying information carrier; however, they are very difficult to control. We have outlined all of the gaps which can be used to inform future work.

title: Real-Time Correlation of Relaxation, Dephasing, and Two-level System Dynamics in Transmon Qubits
abstract: Materials improvements in transmon qubits have yielded remarkable advances in qubit lifetimes (T1)and coherence times (T2). However, state-of-the-art superconducting qubits experience temporal fluctuations in their performance, which limit gate fidelities and quantum processor performance. We observe correlated increases in qubit relaxation and dephasing rates that last for minutes to hours, which we call T1 and T2 excursions. Using interleaved lifetime and coherence time measurements, noise spectroscopy, and two-level-system (TLS) spectroscopy, we find that these excursions are caused by single or few strongly-coupled TLS defects that spectrally diffuse into resonance with the qubit frequency. Our measurement protocol provides a powerful tool for understanding the noise sources that cause temporal fluctuations in superconducting qubit performance.

title: Minimal ancilla for boosting type-I photonic fusion
abstract: Fusion gates enable the creation of large entangled photonic states for linear-optical quantum computing and communication protocols. However, their success probability is limited to $1/2$ without additional photonic resources. Previous schemes for boosting type-I fusion have used four ancillary single photons or a two-qubit Bell state, whose preparation is probabilistic and resource intensive. Here we propose a boosted type-I fusion gate using only two independent ancillary single photons and no entangled ancillary input. It achieves a direct success probability of $5/8$, matching that of the previous four-single-photon proposal while using half as many ancillary photons. The circuit is predominantly passive, with a single active element that applies a phase shift or swaps two modes according to intermediate photodetection outcomes. Unlike the previous schemes, successful outputs occupy fixed modes and require no further conditional output routing. In particular, we show that the gate is more robust to heralded ancillary-photon loss than previously proposed boosted gates and reduces the average number of single photons required to generate a six-qubit ring graph state by more than $4.6\%$ compared with other type-I schemes. It therefore offers a resource-efficient primitive for scalable fusion-based photonic quantum information processing.

title: Feasibility of Distributed Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing: From Quantum Links to Algorithms
abstract: Practical fault-tolerant quantum computation requires a large number of physical qubits, posing a major challenge for scaling up individual quantum processors. Distributed architectures offer a promising solution by interconnecting multiple processors through quantum networks. However, remote Bell-pair generation remains technically demanding, making it essential to assess computational performance under limited communication resources. In this work, we present a comprehensive resource analysis of distributed fault-tolerant quantum computation using superconducting processors connected by microwave or optical links. We show that even a single physical communication channel per node can substantially reduce the physical-qubit requirements per node under experimentally motivated, forward-looking microwave-link assumptions of a 1 MHz physical Bell-pair generation rate and 90% fidelity, although at the cost of a roughly tenfold increase in execution time. Conversely, reducing the execution-time overhead requires substantially greater communication resources, including higher Bell-pair fidelities and extensive multiplexing. These results demonstrate the potential feasibility of distributed fault-tolerant quantum computation with limited communication resources and provide a quantitative basis for balancing quantum-link performance, processor size, and execution time.

title: Efficient Block Encodings of Vibrational Hamiltonians
abstract: Simulation of molecular vibrations is emerging as a promising application of quantum computing in quantum chemistry. In this work, we develop new strategies for block-encoding the second-quantized $n$-mode representation of the vibrational Hamiltonian, whose algebraic structure closely parallels that of the second-quantized electronic Hamiltonian. We derive linear-combination-of-unitaries (LCU) representations of this Hamiltonian based on Pauli decomposition and tensor hypercontraction (THC) and construct efficient circuits for the corresponding block encodings. We also extend the Block-Invariant Symmetry Shift (BLISS) technique to vibrational Hamiltonians, yielding a lower LCU 1-norm and, consequently, a lower overall circuit cost. For the molecules considered here, BLISS-THC reduces the Toffoli cost of quantum phase estimation by more than two orders of magnitude relative to existing block-encoding approaches. In comparison with recent Trotter-based methods, it shows up to a ninefold reduction in the T-gate count, with the relative savings tending to increase with system size. Asymptotically, and up to polylogarithmic factors, both the Pauli and THC LCUs trade additional ancillas for a quadratic improvement in scaling with the number of modes, while THC provides an additional quadratic improvement in scaling with the number of modals. These results highlight the importance of Hamiltonian factorizations and Toffoli-qubit tradeoffs for reducing the computational cost of quantum simulations of molecular vibrations.

title: When is a bosonic operator a Hamiltonian?
abstract: Hermitian polynomials in the quadrature operators $x$ and $p$ are the basic ingredients of continuous-variable quantum information, and increasingly exotic ones are now routinely engineered in superconducting circuits and trapped ions. However, such a polynomial need not define unique quantum dynamics: it may define exactly one, none, or an infinite family of physically distinct ones. Such obstructions are invisible to algebraic arguments and can compromise finite-dimensional truncations, which may fail to converge or silently converge to the wrong dynamics. We develop a method, implemented as an algorithm, which decides which case occurs, and how large the family is, from the coefficients alone, with no functional-analytic input from the user. For Gaussian operators the answer is always one; for non-Gaussian ones, a regime continuous-variable quantum computing cannot do without, the other outcomes occur already for simple and physically natural Hamiltonians. We apply the algorithm to operators drawn from the recent literature.

title: Designing Quantum Solutions to the Closest String Problem with the Non-Variational QWOA
abstract: Quantum computing offers promising approaches to combinatorial optimization problems whose search spaces grow exponentially with problem size. The Closest String problem belongs to this category, which seeks a string that minimizes the maximum Hamming distance to any string in a given collection of reference strings. In this work, we present an end-to-end quantum implementation of the Closest String problem using the Non-Variational Quantum Walk Optimization Algorithm (NV-QWOA), evaluating its resource requirements and solution amplification capabilities. Our automated workflow converts arbitrary problem instances into quantum circuits expressed in one- or two-qubit gates that encode candidate solutions, evaluate the objective function, and apply NV-QWOA optimisation to increase the measurement probabilities of high-quality solutions. Analytical resource estimates yield a qubit complexity of $\mathcal{O}(nm\log k)$ and a circuit depth of $\mathcal{O}(pm\log^2 n + pn\log n)$, where $n$ is the string length, $m$ is the number of reference strings, $k$ is the alphabet size, and $p$ is the number of NV-QWOA iterations. We introduce a revised prescription for the phase-separation parameter, $γ$, that depends on problem size but requires no instance-specific optimization. This prescription mitigates excessive phase wrapping modulo $2π$, which can weaken the relationship between objective values and the phases guiding the optimization dynamics. Across all simulated problem sizes, the algorithm consistently amplifies optimal and near-optimal candidates. This work provides an explicit gate-level implementation, an improved phase-scaling method, and a foundation for hardware experiments and benchmarking against classical algorithms.

title: Variational Quantum Optimization of Noisy Polarization Qubit Experiments
abstract: Quantum networking enables advanced communication protocols, distributed quantum computing, and enhanced sensing. These applications are often hindered by current realizations of quantum network nodes, which utilize noisy and imperfect hardware. Here, we apply variational optimization to counteract the effects of such imperfections. We parameterize network protocols for use with variational methods and then use these methods to optimize simple prepare-and-measure protocols on an optical testbed as a proof-of-principle demonstration. We demonstrate automated polarization compensation, achieving results comparable to conventional methods. We also analyze the effects of hardware imperfections and dark counts on the performance of our optimizations. We compare the performance of various gradient estimation methods and propose natural extensions, including further improvements through the use of global optimization and hybrid gradient estimation methods, as well as the application of variational optimization to nodes deployed on fiber networks.

title: Trial-space co-design for quantum simulation on noisy hardware
abstract: Quantum simulations on noisy hardware are often designed as if the machine were ideal, with device limitations considered only after the basis and measurement plan have been chosen. We instead use information about the physical problem and the device at an earlier stage, to decide which states and evolution times should form a compact simulation basis. Because the target problem remains unchanged, the method adapts only the representation used to solve it. Tests on many-body and molecular models show that this approach can reveal useful directions that ordinary time evolution misses, while also exposing an important limitation: some of these directions can become too similar to estimate reliably. Realistic device data further show that hardware response can change the preferred states and evolution times before execution. Across seven acquisition days, a four-qubit experiment shows a median 54\% reduction in projected-energy error from problem-informed time choices relative to uniform sampling under matched hardware conditions. These results provide a proof of principle for simulation-basis design as a practical interface between quantum algorithms and the hardware that executes them.

title: Direct tests of conformal symmetry with Rydberg atoms: assessment and proposals
abstract: We propose a direct test of conformal symmetry using Rydberg-atom arrays. By arranging the atoms on a circle and measuring equal-time two-point correlation functions, the characteristic functional form predicted by conformal field theory can be tested directly. We estimate the number of experimental snapshots required to resolve this behavior with sufficient statistical precision. We further optimize the time-dependent ramp profile of the Rabi frequency~$Ω$ and detuning~$Δ$ used to prepare the target critical state adiabatically. The optimized profile achieves higher fidelity over much shorter evolution times than those employed in previous experiments. Taken together, these results suggest that a direct experimental test of conformal symmetry is feasible with current Rydberg-atom technology.

title: Low-frustration block encodings by patch routing
abstract: Block-encoding has emerged as a core primitive in many quantum algorithms, including quantum simulation. In this work, we design efficient and extensible methods for generating low-frustration block encodings of frustrated lattice Hamiltonians built from repeated local interaction patches through a technique we call "patch routing". We construct block encodings for a full Hamiltonian by first block-encoding a small local patch and then using a SWAP-style routing network to coherently apply the local patch encoding across the lattice. The expensive, local block-encoding cost is paid only once per query and is independent of lattice size, whereas the comparatively inexpensive routing network grows linearly with the lattice size, dominating at large sizes. Our method allows for a hierarchical structure in which larger patches can be block-encoded with small normalization factors, albeit at a higher (local, non-extensive) block-encoding cost, thereby reducing overall query complexity in an algorithm. We exploit symmetries and algebraic structures in local interactions to construct efficient block encodings, and we apply these techniques to the Heisenberg, Fermi-Hubbard, and honeycomb spin-liquid models. For a $120\times 120$ square-lattice $J_1$-$J_2$ Heisenberg model near maximal frustration ($J_2/J_1=0.4-0.6$), our methods result in a $15-17\times$ reduction in the leading $T$ cost per qubitized-QPE run (ignoring initial state preparation and overlap) relative to prior state-of-the-art Pauli LCU constructions. Corresponding reductions are approximately $3\times$ for the $120\times120$ Fermi-Hubbard model at half-filling. For time evolution of the honeycomb spin-liquid model on $120\times120$ unit cells, the leading cost is reduced by $5\times$. Our framework provides a systematic way forward for larger and more accurate fault-tolerant simulations of real-world quantum systems.

title: Fully quantum training of parametric circuits with Quantum Hamiltonian Descent
abstract: Parametric quantum circuits are usually trained by classical, local optimizers, which use the quantum computer only to evaluate the cost function, or its gradient, one point at a time. Quantum Hamiltonian Descent (QHD) takes a different route: in this quantum algorithm for continuous optimization, the parameters become the position of a quantum particle, with the cost function as its potential, and two time schedules control kinetic and potential energy so that the wavefunction explores the whole landscape and tunnels towards the global minimum. QHD, however, assumes a classically computable cost function, and its digital implementation is poorly understood: standard error bounds grow exponentially with the number of qubits per parameter, and the schedules are borrowed from classical optimization. Here we propose to train parametric circuits with QHD entirely on the quantum computer, through an online step in which the qubits encoding the parameters coherently control the circuit on a second register. We prove that, for cost functions with a smooth periodic extension, including those of parametric circuits, the simulation error admits a bound independent of the grid resolution, and that for circuits the bound grows at most linearly with the number of parameters. We also show that the ideal dynamics depends on the two schedules only through a single curve, which controls the adiabaticity of the search, and that the remaining freedom can be used to minimize the gate count. Simulations on benchmark functions and parametric circuits show that, at equal cost, schedules designed in this way markedly increase the probability of finding the global minimum.

title: Fermion Scattering on Quantum Computers
abstract: Resonant scattering links particle interactions to the formation and decay of unstable excitations. We develop a hybrid quantum-computing framework to study these dynamics through fermion--antifermion collisions. Our formulation of $(1+1)$-dimensional Yukawa theory encodes fermions in qubits and the scalar field in qumodes. We identify the operations needed for a photonic implementation and benchmark the dynamics with tensor-network simulations. Near resonance, we resolve the build-up of a localised scalar excitation and the subsequent partial return of energy to the fermions. Enhanced entanglement accompanies this exchange. Time-dependent correlator measurements reproduce the analytically predicted decay rate to a few percent precision, with energy scans exhibiting a resonance peak consistent with packet-averaged Breit--Wigner behaviour. These results establish a concrete scattering benchmark for hybrid quantum computers and demonstrate how local real-time observables can probe particle-resonance dynamics.

title: Hardware-Friendly Estimation of LCU-Based Expectation Values via Quantum-to-Classical Workload Shifting
abstract: Estimating the expectation value of an observable $O$ for a quantum state evolved under a general, possibly non-unitary, operator $A$ is a fundamental task in quantum simulation, chemistry, and variational algorithms. Existing linear-combination-of-unitaries (LCU) approaches implement $A$ on hardware, requiring ancilla qubits, controlled unitaries and, in randomized variants, fresh circuit executions for every Monte Carlo sample. These costs are prohibitive on NISQ and early fault-tolerant devices. We propose HERMES (Hardware-Efficient Reusable Measurements for Estimating LCU-based expectation valueS), which moves the processing of $A$ entirely to the classical domain. Expanding $A$ and $O$ in the Pauli basis and sampling pairs of Pauli terms classically, HERMES rewrites $μ= \mathrm{Tr}(OAρA^{\dagger})/\mathrm{Tr}(AρA^{\dagger})$ as a ratio of weighted sums of Pauli expectation values on the unmodified state $ρ$, with no ancillas, controlled unitaries, or quantum implementation of $A$. A two-level measurement reduction scheme (Pauli deduplication and commuting-group partitioning) bounds the number of distinct measurement settings independently of the sample count, unlike randomized LCU methods whose circuit executions grow linearly with it. On ground-state energy estimation of $\mathrm{H}_2$ and $\mathrm{LiH}$ via imaginary-time evolution, HERMES matches or beats Pauli single-ancilla LCU baseline using shallow circuits with no two-qubit gates beyond state preparation under qubit-wise commuting grouping. It is also more robust to noise and completes a noisy $\mathrm{LiH}$ simulation infeasible for the baseline, at the cost of classical overhead growing with the number of Pauli terms in $A$.

title: Modular optical fault-tolerant quantum computation via an interface between verified resources and online logical operations
abstract: We introduce a factory--processor interface architecture for modular optical fault-tolerant quantum computation that separates code-dependent encoded-resource preparation from reusable online logical processing on a common Gaussian optical processor. Beyond encoded resources, the interface specifies logical outputs, code-to-mode mapping, measurement roles, frame updates, verification records, and resource-injection boundaries. As a concrete realization, we combine an offline verified Bell-resource factory based on a recursively concatenated $C_4$ code with physical Gottesman--Kitaev--Preskill (GKP) qubits with an online time-domain measurement-based quantum computation (MBQC) processor. Under the specified additive-displacement-noise model and fixed postselection policy, simulations support the finite-level logical Bell-error ordering $P_5<P_4<P_3<P_2$ at 12.25 dB of effective GKP displacement-noise quality, both with and without the prescribed additional post-injection displacement noise. At 15.6 dB and $L=2$, a separate fixed-sample evaluation gives one-sided 95$\%$ Clopper--Pearson upper bounds below $10^{-5}$ for both conditions under the binomial model. The interface supports address-tracked injection, transversal CNOT and logical Bell-measurement constructions, and logical SWAP and Hadamard constructions with tracked code permutations. Given advance resource preparation and sufficient routing parallelism, increasing the concatenation level expands parallel encoded-resource width without increasing the protected online sequence length of these constructions. These results identify a modular route to lower logical error rates while retaining a common Gaussian MBQC operation set with shallow online processing.

title: Quantum Machine Learning in Medical Imaging: A Primer for Radiologists
abstract: Deep learning has transformed radiology, but the computational cost of training and deploying modern models is outpacing what classical hardware can support. Quantum computing has been proposed as one response to this bottleneck: an n-qubit system can represent $2^n$ states simultaneously, although practical speedups require efficient algorithms, data encoding, and measurement strategies rather than superposition alone. This review introduces radiologists to five core quantum concepts, qubits, superposition, entanglement, quantum gates, and quantum circuits, and to the superconducting, trapped-ion, and photonic hardware platforms that define the current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era. We then summarize the quantum machine learning architectures most often applied to medical imaging (quantum support vector machines, quantum neural networks, variational quantum circuits, and quantum convolutional neural networks) and quantum image representations such as the flexible representation of quantum images (FRQI) and the novel enhanced quantum representation (NEQR). Reported applications include brain tumor classification and segmentation on MRI, pneumonia detection on chest radiographs, skin and breast lesion classification, CT and PET reconstruction, and ultrasound denoising. Nearly all published systems are hybrid quantum-classical pipelines evaluated on small, downsampled benchmark datasets or simulators, and clinical deployment is not yet feasible. We conclude with current limitations and translational priorities for radiology.

title: Trace-distance characterization of recurrent pairwise synchronization in cavity-coupled superconducting qubits
abstract: We theoretically investigate recurrent pairwise synchronization in three super?conducting qubits coupled to a common single-mode microwave cavity. The qubits interact indirectly through the cavity field and are driven by a coher?ent microwave field. We obtain the coherent dynamics in the dressed-state basis and quantify pairwise synchronization by the trace distance between reduced single-qubit density matrices. The trace-distance dynamics exhibit oscillatory wave-packet structures, with low-trace-distance regions identifying finite syn?chronization windows. An envelope-threshold procedure is introduced to extract the representative duration of these windows. By varying the middle-qubit coupling strength and the relative coupling ratio of the outer qubits, we con?struct a parameter-dependent map of the synchronization-window duration. The duration decreases rapidly with increasing relative outer-qubit coupling and becomes weakly dependent on the middle-qubit coupling in the stronger-coupling regime. These results provide a reduced-state-based characterization of coherent collective dynamics in multiqubit circuit-QED systems.

title: The Compendium of Super-Quadratic Computational Quantum Advantages
abstract: This compendium presents a structured collection of computational problems with credible prospects for realizing meaningful quantum advantage, focused on describing problem characteristics rather than specific algorithms. It is intended for non-quantum researchers and practitioners with strong computational backgrounds, particularly domain experts, seeking to assess the relevance of quantum methods to real-world problems. The compendium focuses on enumerating core problems for which there is good evidence that a quantum computer can realize more than a quadratic speedup in offline non-relativized time-complexity (e.g., as opposed to in oracular settings, streaming models, or communication advantages). Entries characterize the structural constraints that real-world instances must satisfy to realize those advantages in practice. The intention is to provide a reference that can be leveraged to connect quantum algorithms to practical use cases.

title: LYNX - A trapped-ion quantum information processor
abstract: We introduce LYNX, a quantum information processor based on trapped $^{40}$Ca$^+$ ions. It utilizes up to 31 qubits with all-to-all connectivity. We characterize the system performance using rigorous benchmarks, such as randomized benchmarking (RB), GHZ state fidelity estimates, and quantum volume (QV) tests. The LYNX processor shows average 1-qubit gate errors of $8(5)\times 10^{-5}$ tested via standard RB in a 24-qubit register. An average 2-qubit gate error in a 24-qubit register of $2.84(8)\times 10^{-3}$ is demonstrated using interleaved RB. Furthermore, the device passes QV tests using up to 15 qubits which corresponds to a quantum volume of QV$=2^{15}$.

title: Quantum Secret Sharing from CSS qLDPC Codes: Computable Access Structures, Accessible Logical Dimension, and Topology-Aware Network Cost
abstract: Quantum secret sharing (QSS) schemes can be constructed from quantum error-correcting codes, but characterizing their access structures and implementation costs becomes challenging for finite-length, high-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes. We develop an exact computational framework for QSS induced by CSS qLDPC codes. The framework characterizes authorized, forbidden, and intermediate coalitions using restricted parity-check matrices and binary linear algebra, and introduces the accessible logical dimension \(κ(A)\), defined through the symplectic rank of locally supported logical classes, to refine the characterization of intermediate coalitions. We further incorporate physical network constraints through separate Tanner-incidence, Steiner-routing, and scheduling-depth costs, and treat the partitioning of physical qubits into participants as an explicit design variable. Numerical experiments on four CSS qLDPC codes verify the predicted complement duality and monotonicity properties and show substantial variation in access transitions and network costs. For the codes studied, the bivariate bicycle instance exhibits the sharpest transition, while network embedding costs vary by more than an order of magnitude across physical topologies. We also show that participant partitioning can substantially improve block-level security and reconstruction thresholds. These results provide a practical bridge between the algebraic structure of CSS qLDPC codes, the graded accessibility of quantum secrets, and the physical constraints of networked QSS implementations.

title: Entangled logical qubits on a superconducting quantum processor
abstract: We demonstrate high-fidelity logical qubit operations using \texttt{ibm\_phoenix}, a square-lattice array of 120 coupled superconducting qubits that are capable of fast reset. Using strategies to exclude underperforming components together with noise informed decoding, we routinely produce surface codes at distance-3 and distance-5 with logical error per round below 1\%. We demonstrate entanglement between two logical qubits, where logical Bell-state fidelities above 93\% are observed for entanglement created via lattice surgery. With three logical qubits and lattice surgery, we perform logical teleportation of a range of states and gates, observing fidelities in the range 78\% - 93\%. Using reset to reduce qubit leakage, we show that repeated rounds of stabilizer measurements continue to exhibit improvements in a stability experiment up to $\sim 2\cdot 10^{-7}$ over 170 measurement rounds.

title: Two-Layer Verification for Fault-Tolerant Magic-State Preparation in High-Rate Quantum Codes
abstract: Encoded magic states are essential for universal fault-tolerant quantum computation, but their resource-efficient preparation in high-rate quantum codes remains challenging. To address this limitation, we propose two-layer verification, which combines local verification of independently prepared subblocks with logical verification after their embedding into a target code. This hierarchy detects harmful error patterns, including even-parity logical-eigenvalue flips that are invisible to a collective product check alone. We demonstrate this scheme for a $[[21,3,5]]$ code by constructing a circuit that embeds three verified seven-qubit Steane-code magic states into the target code. Circuit-level simulations of $T$- and $S$-state preparation show logical-error suppression consistent with the code distance. These results demonstrate the potential of two-layer verification as a design principle for reliable magic-state preparation in quantum codes encoding multiple logical qubits.

title: Performing a Quantum Subroutine Using Cluster States
abstract: Quantum subroutines, like their classical counterparts, serve as essential components of larger algorithms. They can be realized using gate based architectures or measurement based quantum computation (MBQC), where computation proceeds through adaptive measurements on highly entangled cluster states. In this work, we implement a phase oracle as a reusable subroutine within the MBQC framework using experimentally feasible cluster states. Unlike prior demonstrations of Grover's algorithm in MBQC that omit explicit oracle construction, our approach provides a transparent formulation of the oracle subroutine, including its measurement patterns, byproduct correlations, density-matrix simulations, and corresponding MBQC measurement circuits.

title: Single-step SU(3) Hahn Echo in a Qutrit Atom Interferometer
abstract: The Hahn echo is a well-known dynamical decoupling method that refocuses the dephasing due to energy inhomogeneities of a spin-1/2 ensemble and is widely used to extend phase coherence in quantum computers and sensors. Extensions of such techniques beyond the spin-1/2 have been reported, but have mainly used SU(2) gates, limiting their scalability. Here, we generalize the Hahn echo to qutrits using single-step SU(3) gates and extend the coherence time by more than an order of magnitude. The gates are generated through optimal control theory and implemented in an ultracold atomic ensemble in free fall. A quantum process tomography procedure benchmarks the gates and yields fidelities of ~ 93%, limited mainly by state preparation and measurement errors. Due to the geometry of the laser beams, the generalized Hahn echo also realizes a three-path Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometer with two independent interferometric phase differences. Our results therefore establish SU(3) control for dynamical decoupling of qutrits and multi-path atom interferometers, with the latter opening the possibility for vector force measurements and interferometric tests of the validity of Born's rule.

title: Photon-Number Discrimination from Increasing Time-of-Arrival Separation in Wide Superconducting Microstrip Single-Photon Detectors
abstract: Measurements of photon-number-dependent time-of-arrival (TOA) distributions in wide NbN superconducting microstrip single-photon detectors (SMSPDs) are presented. Two \SI{10}{\um}-long devices with widths of \SI{3.2}{\um} and \SI{6.4}{\um} are characterized under pulsed \SI{515}{nm} excitation. The TOA histograms are described by sums of exponentially modified Gaussian (EMG) components, with the wider device exhibiting components assigned to photon numbers up to \(n=8\). Adjacent TOA peaks become more distinguishable relative to their widths at higher photon number, in contrast to the compression of neighboring photon-number timing shifts observed in conventional narrow-wire SNSPDs. For the components assigned to \(n=7\) and \(n=8\), the FWHM-normalized peak separation is \(2.15\), and the fitted EMG distributions yield an equal-prior pairwise TOA-assignment fidelity of \(99.6\%\). The EMG exponential-tail parameter \(τ_n\) decreases strongly with photon number, while the Gaussian-location parameter \(μ_n\) continues to shift between neighboring components. A phenomenological model motivated by absorption-site-dependent vortex processes and collective current redistribution captures these timing trends. These results support wide SMSPDs as a platform for TOA-based photon-number discrimination at high photon number, relevant to multiphoton-state characterization and photonic quantum information processing. The same geometry also provides a setting to examine how the spatial distribution of photon absorption affects vortex-assisted detection.

title: Trident: Efficient Load Verification for Yoked Surface Codes using a Three-Level Memory Hierarchy
abstract:
Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computers (FTQCs) commonly use the surface code to encode program qubits as error-corrected logical qubits. Unfortunately, the surface code has a poor encoding rate, so recent work has proposed Yoked Surface Codes (YSCs), which concatenate the surface code with a high-rate quantum code. The surface code qubits in YSCs are protected by the checks, or yokes, of the high-rate code. YSCs have 1D and 2D variants, which are $1.8\times$ and $4.5\times$ more efficient than the surface code, respectively.
  Modern FTQC architectures use a two-level hierarchy: surface codes perform logical operations (compute) while 2D YSCs store idle program qubits (memory). To load a qubit from memory, the FTQC first performs retrieval, which logically moves a program qubit from a 2D YSC into a surface code (8 cycles). However, retrieval is not fault-tolerant, so the FTQC must verify the load by measuring all the yokes of the 2D YSC (178 cycles). As verification dominates memory access latency, eliminating it can provide a speedup of $5.7\times$.
  Our goal is to reduce the verification overhead of 2D YSCs while retaining their storage efficiency. We exploit the fact that 1D YSCs, though less storage-efficient, incur negligible verification latency. We propose Trident, which expands the two-level hierarchy into a three-level hierarchy by adding a small intermediate level containing a 1D YSC (L1). If most loads hit L1 rather than L2 (2D YSC tier), it can significantly reduce verification overhead. We present two variants: Trident-D (demand-driven) and Trident-P (prefetch-driven), which achieve speedups of $2.8\times$ and $4.2\times$, respectively, while increasing the physical qubit cost of memory by only 4.9%.

title: Quantum Cryptomania with Classical Communication without One-Way Functions
abstract:
In classical cryptography, one-way functions are necessary for most of cryptography. In the quantum world, however, Kretschmer at {TQC'21} and subsequent works have demonstrated that quantum versions of various primitives in minicrypt, such as signatures and private-key encryption, do not require quantum-computable one-way functions (\textsf{qOWF}s). However, the question of the necessity of \textsf{qOWF}s for primitives in Cryptomania like public-key encryption with classical public keys and ciphertexts (\textsf{qPKE}) has remained open.
  We provide a comprehensive picture of the relationship between \textsf{qPKE} and \textsf{qOWF}. First, our main result is a black-box separation between \textsf{qOWF}s and \textsf{qPKE}. In particular, we show that relative to a unitary, real, and self-inverse oracle, there exists a \textsf{qPKE} scheme (with classical keys and ciphertexts), but \textsf{qOWF}s do not exist. Further, our oracles admit a point-function obfuscation construction, thus ruling out black-box construction of \textsf{qOWF} from point function obfuscations.
  On the positive side, we construct \textsf{qPKE} from quantum indistinguishability obfuscation for quantum circuits with classical obfuscated descriptions and efficiently verifiable one-way puzzles, which is known to be a potentially weaker assumption than \textsf{qOWF}s, due to an existing black-box separation. Our construction is the quantum analog of the classical construction of \textsf{PKE} from one-way functions and indistinguishability obfuscation in the quantum computation with classical communication (QCCC) setting.

title: Robustness of Quantum Correlations and Controlled Teleportation Fidelity under Noisy Channels
abstract: In distributed quantum computing, quantum networks provide a potential infrastructure for long-range quantum information processing. Controlled quantum teleportation (CQT) is a key practically relevant protocol that can connect two parties on a network and enables a third party, the controller to allow or abort the secure teleportation of an arbitrary single-qubit state between the two parties. We investigate the robustness of a three-qubit GHZ resource under bit-flip, phase-flip, depolarizing, and amplitude-damping noise. Using the Kraus-operator formalism, we characterize the noisy resource through multipartite quantum discord, genuine multipartite concurrence (GMC), localizable entanglement (LE), and CQT fidelity. We also outline a proof-of-concept photonic implementation for preparing the three-qubit GHZ resource and realizing the CQT protocol, which could enable experimental investigation of the effects of noise. Our results show that bit-flip and amplitude-damping noise generally preserve useful mutipartite quantum correlations over broader noise parameter ranges. Interestingly, multipartite discord exhibits freezing under bit-flip noise over a finite parameter regime. Moreover, discord can persist beyond the sudden death of genuine multipartite entanglement, revealing the distinct robustness of nonclassical correlations. We further demonstrate that CQT fidelity which characterizes the performance of CQT can exceed the classical threshold even after GMC vanishes, while LE more closely reflects the operational usefulness of the noisy resource. These findings highlight the complementary roles of quantum correlations and entanglement in assessing the resilience of GHZ-based protocols.

title: Optimal Control of a Fluxonium Circuit with the Q-PRONTO Numerical Method
abstract: Optimizing the control of large quantum systems is a resource-intensive task, where the convergence rate of the underlying iterative schemes is crucial. The recently developed Quantum Projection Operator-Based Newton Method for Trajectory Optimization (Q-PRONTO) offers a unique quadratic convergence for controlling quantum states, while most model-based solvers guarantee only an approximately linear convergence rate. As a proof of concept, here, we design and benchmark single-qubit gates optimized by Q-PRONTO based on the circuit Hamiltonian of a fluxonium superconducting qubit. To ensure that we can apply a long string of arbitrary pulses to the circuit, we modify the firmware associated with the Quantum Instrumentation Control Kit (QICK) by altering its memory allocation. We characterize the performance of the optimal solutions using standard randomized benchmarking and achieve a total error per gate of $6.6\times10^{-4}$.

title: Temporal Degeneracy Limits Message Passing Decoding of QLDPC Codes Under Repeated Noisy Syndrome Measurements
abstract: Practical quantum computations can require logical error rates of $10^{-12}$ or lower. Quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes are promising candidates for reaching such rates with low qubit overhead, provided that their syndromes can be decoded efficiently. Repeated noisy syndrome measurements introduce temporal degeneracy into the space-time decoding graph. We characterize the temporal kernel, whose vectors have zero total data parity, and show that it is generated by elementary temporal codewords of weight $d_v+2$, where $d_v$ is the variable-node degree. For $(d_v,d_c)$-regular parity-check matrices with fixed degrees $d_v,d_c>2$ and girth greater than four, we derive counting bounds and construct degenerate error patterns of weight $(d_v+2)/2$ for even $d_v$ and $d_v+1$ for odd $d_v$, with multiplicity $Θ(nr)$ in the blocklength $n$ and number of measurement rounds $r$. Under the isolation assumption, these patterns cause local failures of deterministic isotropic message-passing decoders under a flooding schedule. These failures depend on the node degrees rather than the minimum distance; for the bivariate bicycle (BB) codes considered, their weight is equal to four. Monte carlo simulations and fixed-weight importance sampling quantify harmful low-weight degenerate error patterns for the min-sum (MS) decoder beyond the isolation assumption. Motivated by the identified symmetries, we propose space-time anisotropic min-sum decoding with syndrome-guided realizations. Its complexity is linear in the number of Tanner graph edges for fixed maximum number of iterations and number of decoders. Numerical results on BB codes show threshold-like behavior acrossthe tested code sizes and improved failure probabilities relative to MS decoding with ordered statistics decoding post-processing.

title: The Entire Quantum Computer on a Classical Leash
abstract:
We show that a classical client with no quantum hardware can use a single untrusted and potentially malicious quantum server as if it were its own trusted quantum computer. Through the server, the client can privately choose and run quantum computations, prepare quantum states, and process quantum states supplied by other parties. It can also keep quantum memory on the server, hidden from the server itself, and use that memory in later computations so its quantum state persists across rounds of interaction. Together, these capabilities let a purely classical party act as a quantum party in a variety of interactive protocols.
  We expect this virtual quantum computer to be a broadly useful tool. As immediate applications, we resolve two known open problems: (1) classical verification of quantum sampling with negligible computational soundness error, and (2) remote state preparation of arbitrary efficiently preparable quantum states.
  Underlying all of these results is a general-purpose, maliciously secure two-party computation protocol between a classical client and a quantum server, which we construct assuming only the post-quantum hardness of learning with errors.

title: Screening strongly correlated materials in solid oxide cells with quantum simulation
abstract: We develop an end-to-end framework for assessing a quantum-computing application in industrial materials science: the screening of strongly correlated oxygen-electrode materials for SOFCs and SOECs. We formulate the materials problem in terms of interface observables including oxygen-vacancy formation energies, vacancy migration barriers, and electronic conductivity. We describe how these observables can be obtained using a diagrammatic GW-based embedding, either GW+DMFT or self-energy embedding theory (SEET), applied to a DFT-screened shortlist. The atomistic electrode/electrolyte interface defines the electronic structure problem from which the correlated impurity models are constructed. Quantum impurity solvers would provide the finite-temperature impurity Green's functions required by the embedding. The computational challenges that classical solvers may encounter as the interacting active space grows, together with the polynomial scaling of quantum Hamiltonian simulation for efficiently represented discretized models, open an opportunity for quantum advantage. We identify the benchmarks needed to assess this opportunity through convergence of vacancy and migration energetics and comparison with the best applicable classical solvers. We provide illustrative logical qubit counts and identify the thermal state preparation, simulation, measurement, and repeated-solve costs needed for a complete resource assessment. We connect microscopic observables to macroscopic engineering metrics using a continuum model for mixed ionic--electronic conducting oxygen electrodes that couples oxygen surface exchange, solid-state oxygen transport, electrode microstructure, and finite electrode thickness. Finally, we estimate the potential worldwide business value of improved electrode materials under SOFC and SOEC deployment scenarios informed by public technical targets and electrolyser deployment data.

title: Problem-aware sampling for bias and variance reduction in randomised Hamiltonian simulation
abstract: Randomised quantum simulation algorithms such as qDRIFT reduce circuit depth by replacing deterministic product formulas with stochastic compilations, but achieving high accuracy can require many steps. In vanilla qDRIFT, Hamiltonian terms are sampled with probabilities proportional to their coefficient magnitudes. We propose StateDRIFT, a variant of qDRIFT which optimises its sampling distribution to estimate time-evolved quantities using knowledge of the initial state and target observable, with a provable truncation bound that keeps qDRIFT's guarantees. The distribution at each depth is chosen by solving an optimisation problem targeting bias and/or variance. StateDRIFT can significantly reduce the bias and variance of estimators, and hence circuit depth, which we test on short-time dynamics of lattice models and molecules under Jordan-Wigner up to 18 qubits. For example, with BeH2 StateDRIFT can reduce the number of two-qubit gates required to achieve a given accuracy from 11,201 to 983. StateDRIFT involves measuring observables and commutators on the initial state, so we propose two practical ways to estimate these: classical surrogates such as tensor networks, and classical shadows, which recover most or all of the saving from exact oracles in the systems tested.

title: ConQEC: Concolic Testing for Quantum Error-Correcting Code Implementations
abstract: Quantum error-correcting code (QECC) implementations are hybrid software-control systems: measured syndromes drive decoder dispatch, recovery actions, and logical checks. Existing QECC verification techniques can prove formal obligations, and general quantum testing can expose final failures, but developers still lack a scalable testing workflow that generates concrete faults and explains where a QECC repair path first diverges. This paper presents ConQEC, to our knowledge the first concolic testing framework for QECC implementations. By combining concrete (Pauli) fault replay with symbolic repair-path constraints, ConQEC generates tests that expose not only final logical failures but also fault--syndrome--decoder--recovery (FSDR) diagnostics: the injected fault, observed syndrome, decoder decision, recovery action, oracle result, and earliest divergent stage. Its symbolic encoding of Pauli faults, syndrome predicates, decoder and recovery relations, and oracle checks enables this diagnostic workflow to scale beyond exponentially increasing amplitude-level quantum-state reasoning. We implemented ConQEC and evaluated it on generated source-level QECC families and public QECC artifacts with up to thousands of qubits. ConQEC detects the seeded bug in every experimental case and reports a replay-valid, fault-localizing FSDR witness for each.

title: Automating quantum circuit optimization with AI agents
abstract: Compiling quantum algorithms for real devices involves hard optimization problems that can decide whether an algorithm runs at scale. We present a general method for solving such problems with AI agents, with every result certified. It builds on autoresearch loops, in which agents iteratively improve programs against a fixed evaluator and which have recently improved quantum cryptanalysis circuits, and adds two elements: a frozen, exact verifier certifies every result, and this verifier, together with the challenge around it, is built by an agent that formulates the problem with a researcher and validates the verifier against a solved case, deliberately broken solutions and published results before any solution exists. The method applies to any optimization problem whose solutions can be verified exactly and efficiently. We apply it to three compilation problems in quantum simulation, namely fermion-to-qubit encoding, Hamiltonian layout and unitary synthesis. In each, the agents improved substantially on published or standard constructions, reducing the cost being optimized by up to 73% at the largest sizes tested and outperforming a state-of-the-art optimizer for fermion-to-qubit encodings. Every submission is a program accompanied by its agent's notes, so the ideas behind each improvement are recorded in human-readable form; later agents built on them, and we describe them here. These results open the way to automated, certified discovery across quantum circuit design and beyond.

title: The limits of magic-state distillation
abstract: Magic-state factories are a major cost of fault-tolerant quantum computing, yet how few noisy inputs they need is known only for restricted protocols. We show that, for tolerating input faults, any stabilizer protocol, however adaptive, postselected or multistage, is no better than a projection onto one stabilizer code, and that for rational targets a fault pattern is harmful exactly when its complement is. Searches over all codes show that quadratic distillation of one T state needs exactly nine inputs and that the eight-input CCZ factory is optimal. At order $d$, one T state needs $n\geq2d$.

title: Norm-Aware Product Formulas for Hamiltonian Simulations
abstract: With the target of efficiently solving the quantum-mechanical Schrödinger equation on future quantum computers, first- and second-order product formulas for the time-evolution operator are proposed, designed to exploit hierarchies in the operator norms of the individual Hamiltonian components. Inspired by the THRIFT product formula, these decomposition schemes achieve a suppression of the leading error term by a factor of alpha<1 with respect to the standard Lie--Trotter--Suzuki splitting of the same order, where alpha quantifies the norm ratio between the dominant and subdominant parts of the Hamiltonian. Unlike THRIFT, the proposed formulas retain the general product-formula structure, making them applicable to Hamiltonians whose terms act on an arbitrary number of qubits. The advantages of this approach are demonstrated through numerical experiments on engineered two-dimensional spin-1/2 XY model systems and isolated molecules within the double-factorization framework.

title: Noise redistribution by stabilizer codes: an organizing view of concatenated three-qubit codes
abstract: We present an organizing framework for concatenated quantum error correction based on the observation that the syndrome projection of a stabilizer code reshapes the noise channel in a code-determined manner. For any stabilizer code, one level of QEC maps the physical noise to a block-diagonal logical channel whose diagonal Pauli weights are fixed by the code geometry. Coherences between different syndrome classes vanish, and no physical Pauli twirl is required to reach this block-diagonal form. Concatenation can then be viewed as the iteration of the same redistribution step: the dominant logical error after one level selects the code used at the next. We instantiate the framework with the two smallest stabilizer codes, the bit-flip and phase-flip codes, and apply it to amplitude damping. The redistribution rules give the concatenation protocol $C_2(\hatσ_y) C_1(\hatσ_x)$, whose ideal-recovery fidelity scales as $f_l=1-\mathcal O(γ^2)$. Solving the crossover condition $F_l>F_{l-1}$ in the ideal-gate limit yields a critical damping parameter $γ_c\approx0.30$; in terms of the initial channel fidelity, $f=1-1.72755γ^2$. Under the same ideal-recovery assumption, we compare the overall gate accuracy rate with that of the five-qubit code. The scope of the framework, in particular for coherent and correlated noise, is stated explicitly.

title: Mode-Selective Micromotion Compensation via Coherent Excitation of a Ground-State-Cooled Motional Mode
abstract: Excess micromotion induced by stray DC electric fields limits the control fidelity of trapped-ion experiments. Various techniques have been developed to detect and compensate ion displacements from the RF null by monitoring modulated fluorescence, ion positions, or micromotion sidebands. Although these approaches are effective, they do not probe the displacement through a ground-state-cooled motional mode and therefore offer limited compatibility with quantum-enhanced sensing protocols. Here, we demonstrate a micromotion compensation method based on the driven coherent amplitude of a ground-state-cooled motional mode. In this approach, the ion displacement is converted into a coherent motional excitation by an auxiliary RF drive and detected through the qubit. We determine the optimal compensation field with a $1σ$ statistical uncertainty of 8 mV/m. The method is naturally compatible with quantum-enhanced sensing protocols employing nonclassical motional states, including Fock, squeezed, and Schrödinger-cat states, providing a pathway toward quantum-enhanced micromotion compensation.

title: Normal-Form Characterization of Adaptivity and Entanglement in Pauli-Based Computation
abstract: Pauli-based computation (PBC) is a measurement-based model of quantum computation that samples from output distributions of universal Clifford+$T$ circuits. Here, we provide a normal form (NF) that completely characterizes its adaptive and entanglement structures. These insights unify PBC with one-way quantum computing as dual or `time-reversed' counterparts. We use the NF to advance strategies for distributed computation and investigate magic-state injection rates. We also demonstrate an exponential improvement in the detection of unnecessary magic-state qubits, allowing their efficient removal. Our NF further enables ahead-of-time circuit compilation using PBC, reducing CNOT gate count and quantum memory of random quantum circuits on average by 50% and 40%, respectively, beating other state-of-the-art compilers.

title: Non-adiabatic Optimisation via Localisation-Delocalisation Transitions
abstract: The promise of efficiently solving classical optimisation problems on quantum computers is tantalizing. As many such problems can be mapped to approximating the ground state of spin-glasses, paradigmatic models for studying many-body localisation, it is natural to ask if some of the intuition coming from quantum statistical mechanics can help guide the construction of novel quantum optimisation algorithms. In this work, we discuss how continuous reverse quantum annealing crossing a many-body localisation transition can be accelerated by considering the density of Landau-Zener crossings as the system is quenched. We provide an interpretation of this behaviour in terms of an effective Fokker-Planck equation for the success probability of the algorithm. This interpretation suggests an improvement in the required annealing time as a function of the system size $N$, which goes from $\mathcal{O}({\rm poly}(N))$ to $\mathcal{O}(1)$ for reference states with non-vanishing energy density. We show that the continuous dynamics can be Trotterised with a number of steps that remains modest as system size increases, making it appealing for near-term devices. For the resulting circuit implementation, we provide a quantitative strategy for determining the parameters of the time-dependent Hamiltonian. We compare the performance of our digitised algorithm, which we call FRIO, against that of the QAOA for finding the ground state of spin-glass problems, in particular the SK model. The numerical results suggest that with suitably selected circuit parameters which can be efficiently found using thermalizing dynamics, FRIO almost always outperforms the conventional QAOA ansatz with pre-optimized angles.

title: Injection is all you need: parallel universal logic in high-rate concatenated self-dual codes
abstract: We propose a quantum architecture that achieves addressable and parallel universal fault-tolerant logical in high-rate codes. The codes are obtained from the flexible concatenation of small-distance high-rate self-dual CSS codes. Addressable and parallel universal logic on the resulting $K$ logical qubits is injected by fault-tolerantly preparing and then consuming diverse logical $K$-qubit CSS stabilizer states and logical $\lvert H \rangle^{\otimes K}$ global magic states. Flag-at-origin is used to prepare the stabilizer resource states while a concatenated cultivation protocol prepares the global magic states. These resource states are consumed by Steane-QEC or Knill-QEC teleportation gadgets, which simultaneously perform quantum error correction. Any quantum algorithm with $T$-depth $D_T$ can be executed by consuming $12D_T$ or fewer resource states. We benchmark the fault-tolerant preparation of the resource states for several two-level concatenations of the $[[k+4,k,2]]$ H codes and the Hamming $[[15,7,3]]$ code. In particular, we find that the concatenated cultivation offers at least one order of magnitude spacetime reduction compared to cultivation in the surface code.

title: High-fidelity and robust controlled-Z gates for superconducting transmon qubits. I. Intrinsic errors and decoherence
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires quantum gates that combine short duration, high fidelity, and robustness to noise. As quantum processors scale, robustness becomes increasingly important because exhaustive characterization and frequent recalibration of individual gates become impractical. We present a comprehensive optimal-control framework for controlled-Z (CZ) gates between directly coupled, frequency-tunable transmons that systematically accounts for intrinsic Hamiltonian errors and realistic decoherence mechanisms, including energy relaxation and dephasing. Using smooth, single-shot flux pulses, we obtain 12-ns CZ gates---close to the theoretical speed limit of 11.6 ns---with intrinsic errors suppressed to the $2\times10^{-5}$ level. We construct dephasing noise models, calibrated against published experimental measurements, that capture fast dephasing from room-temperature control electronics and slow dephasing from $1/f$ flux noise. Using these models, we identify dephasing sweet spots that suppress sensitivity to dephasing noise. We further exploit transmon asymmetry as a design parameter to access distinct noise-resilient operating regimes. These results establish an experimentally applicable framework for balancing gate speed, fidelity, and noise robustness while reducing characterization and recalibration overhead.

title: Meter-scale quantum interconnects between large quantum processors
abstract: Modular quantum architecture requires long-distance quantum interconnects to stitch together individual processor modules. Such interconnects, long-distance couplers or L-couplers, must support coherent quantum operation over meter-scale distances and scale to multiple connections between any two modules. Here we demonstrate four L-couplers operating between two 120-qubit IBM Nighthawk R1 superconducting qubit processors. Each L-coupler joins two Nighthawk lattice qubits through two frequency-tunable L-qubits, two RF-SQUID based "i2m" couplers, and 80 cm of superconducting aluminum coax. Each cable installs perpendicular to the processor surface, to enable denser connections, and is joined to the chip by an indium-to-indium room temperature pressure bond made after both modules were mounted. L-coupler modes near 5 GHz, with internal quality factors of 0.86 to 1.09e6, carry relay-based state transfer at a mean network benchmarking fidelity of 99.00%, with a best link of 99.29 +/- 0.07%. We then realize distant CZ gates between lattice qubits in separate modules at a mean fidelity of 94.75%, with a best link of 96.42 +/- 0.28%, and use them to generate entangled states across the two processors, including a demonstration of simultaneous Bell pair generation using two adjacent L-couplers. These four high-fidelity L-couplers establish a practical path to scalable quantum interconnects for modular quantum computing.

title: Resource Analysis of Quantum Optimization Algorithms via Variational Methods
abstract: Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) are promising approaches for solving combinatorial optimization problems on near-term quantum devices. However, the role played by quantum resources such as entanglement and coherence during the optimization process remains poorly understood. In this work, we investigate the evolution of these resources in two VQAs--the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) and the Feedback-based Algorithm for Quantum Optimization (FALQON)--applied to the Minimum Vertex Cover problem. We employ a variational resource-quantification framework based on the Bures metric and Uhlmann's theorem, in which an auxiliary quantum circuit is optimized to identify the closest resource-free states. This approach allows us to quantify Bures entanglement and Bures coherence of the algorithmic states without requiring full quantum state tomography. For the considered problem instance, QAOA exhibits a pronounced accumulation of entanglement in its initial layers, followed by a progressive reduction as the algorithm converges toward the optimal solution. Its coherence likewise decreases overall with increasing circuit depth, although a finite residual value persists due to the degeneracy of the optimal-solution subspace. In contrast, FALQON exhibits a substantially lower entanglement peak, reached at larger circuit depth, followed by a decay as convergence proceeds. Its coherence decreases smoothly and monotonically together with the optimization error. These results reveal distinct quantum-resource trajectories associated with the two optimization strategies and illustrate how entanglement and coherence evolve as variational quantum states approach solutions of a classical combinatorial optimization problem.

title: Lean-QuantumAlg: A Framework for AI Agents to Produce Quantum Algorithms that Humans Can Trust
abstract: AI agents are increasingly capable of constructing quantum algorithms and proofs, yet machine-checked proofs alone cannot guarantee that the intended problem is solved or that resource claims match the verified computation. Here we introduce Lean-QuantumAlg, a Lean 4 framework for trustworthy AI-assisted development of quantum algorithms. Its Algorithm-Solves-Problem contract binds correctness, success probability, borrowed-state restoration and quantum and classical resource bounds to a single execution, while separating the guarantees that Lean checks from the problem specifications and execution models that humans review. We demonstrate the framework on nine AI-formalized quantum algorithms, from Grover search to quantum attacks on RSA-2048 and P-256, with less than 1% of each algorithm's imported source code requiring statement-level human review once the shared framework has been audited. By integrating reusable mathematical foundations, certified algorithmic primitives and execution-grounded verification, Lean-QuantumAlg provides a basis for AI agents to construct and certify quantum algorithms, opening a path toward scalable AI-driven discovery of quantum algorithms.
